name: Danish
confidence_why: Rischel 1970 and 1982 set out the weight rule for Danish simplex words (a long vowel takes the stress, otherwise the last closed full-vowel syllable, schwa never stressed), Iosad 2016 independently calls the system quantity-sensitive with stress on the rightmost closed syllable, and Grønnum 1998 and Basbøll 2003 likewise describe stress as free but largely predictable with only a handful of lexical minimal pairs; the sole dissent is Gordon 2002's typological appendix, which lists Danish as fixed initial stress on a survey coding that no first-hand description supports.
catalog_citation: Rischel, Jørgen (1982). On unit accentuation in Danish - and the distinction between deep and surface phonology. ARIPUC (Annual Report of the Institute of Phonetics, University of Copenhagen) 16: 191-239.
catalog_locator: pp. 198-200 (section (2), inherent stress placement in polysyllabic morphemes / simplex words); pp. 8-10 of 49; pp. 198-199 read as rendered page scan
catalog_quote: [p.198] ... stress placement is to a considerable extent predictable from surface segmental structure. The strongest generalization is that if one syllable has a long vowel, the stress falls on this syllable. Otherwise there is a rank-ordering so that (with the exception of certain loans from French) a closed syllable takes precedence over an open [p.199] syllable in attracting the stress. ... the second principle takes care of the final stress in forms such as parýk 'wig', stakít 'railing', parasól, but there is a more general prevalence of final stress if the last syllable is closed, cf. komplót 'plot', bandít 'rascal' (this is certainly not without numerous exceptions, however). If the final syllable is open (and the vowel short), the stress is non-final: fóto, gálla (with a short l) ... The accentuation of a variety of structure types is thus predictable, cf. the following examples …
sweep_summary: Danish is in the catalog as weight-hedged on Rischel 1982 (ARIPUC 16:198-199). Ten title-matched items judged: three Rischel papers (1970, 1972, 1982 + its 1983 Folia Linguistica reprint) are about Danish word stress; Iosad 2016 and Basbøll 2003 are stød papers with incidental stress statements; Ejskjær 1990 (stød/pitch accents), Grønnum 1990 (intonation) and Schrambke 2007 (rhythm typology) are prosody but not word stress; Kristiansen 2009 (sociolinguistic 'accents') is irrelevant. downloaded and read today: Rischel 1982 (fresh tidsskrift.dk download; the deciding quotation is verbatim on pp. 198-199), Iosad 2016 (author-hosted CC-BY copy; p. 261 says Danish stress is quantity-sensitive, closed syllables attract stress, 'stress on rightmost closed syllable' in kalif) and Basbøll 2003 (SDU accepted manuscript; says each simplex lexeme has one [stress] syllable, lexically specified or by a 'Default stress rule' it does not spell out - silent on placement). Already held by the project and re-read: Rischel 1970 (full ordered rules 2.1-A.C, 2.2-A.E: schwa never stressed, long vowel wins, else last closed/full vowel - refines), Rischel 1972 (compounds; fn.1 restates 1970 - confirms), Grønnum 1998 JIPA (stress free but largely predictable - confirms). Not obtainable: Rischel 1983 reprint (De Gruyter, paywalled; low priority since the 1982 text is held), Ejskjær 1990 (T&F closed, low), Grønnum 1990/Schrambke 2007/Kristiansen 2009 (abstracts read, none). Nothing read contradicts the catalog; no reclassification indicated. Best first-hand statement: Rischel 1970 rules (pp. 119-122, 129), which do not supersede but underpin the 1982 deciding passage. all discovery went through DOI/Crossref/OpenAlex/Unpaywall/CORE APIs and direct downloads.

new_statements.quote: The placement of stress on one or another syllable of monomorphemic wordforms is to a high extent predictable from the syllable number and syllable structure of their phonetic representations. ... Rule 2.1.-A Syllables with shwa are never stressed. ... Rule 2.1.-B A long vowel in a stressed monomorphemic wordform carries the stress. ... Rule 2.1.-C A stressed monomorphemic wordform which contains no long vowel, takes stress on the last full vowel that is followed by a consonant. ... Rule 2.2.-E If rules 2.2.-A&B&C&D have applied vacuously, the last full vowel is stressed.
new_statements.citation: Rischel, Jørgen (1970). Morpheme stress in Danish. ARIPUC (Annual Report of the Institute of Phonetics, University of Copenhagen) 4: 111-144.
new_statements.reading: Explicit ordered rule set for simplex Danish words: schwa syllables are never stressed; a long vowel takes the stress wherever it is; failing that, the last full vowel that is closed by a consonant (surface formulation) or, in the underlying formulation, long consonant > clusters > default last full vowel. Unbounded, weight-driven (CVV > CVC > CV), with named exception classes (French loans stressed on a short open final, foreign names with antepenult stress, closed-final words with non-final stress). This is the primary statement that the catalog's deciding passage (Rischel 1982:198-199, re-verified today in a fresh download) summarises; it supports the 'weight-hedged' coding and the weight-sensitive (tentative) hedge exactly. Iosad 2016:261 ('the stress system of Danish is quantity-sensitive.. kalif, stress on rightmost closed syllable') is the newest independent confirmation read in this search of works with stress in the title.

new_statements.quote: Stress is free in Danish, but its lexical distinctive function is limited, i.e. stress location in a word is to a considerable extent predictable from phonological and morphological factors. Thus, there are a maximum of perhaps 20-30 minimal stress pairs, e.g. [...] billigst, bilist; August, august; tekniker, teknikker [...]. But stress location in, e.g., the following words is predictably located (indicated for the present purpose in the spelling) 'ælte, 'hule, 'usus, 'eventyr, 'fedekalv, me'lasse, maka'roni, 'tegningerne, 'elskede, be'kende, pro'saisk, 'Panama, ge'bærde, trompe'tist, maler'inde, 'tyndest, 'kvindelig, li'noleumet, bala'lajkaer, 'turbanen, 'skorstensfejer.

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog's coded rule (Gordon 2002 'Initial', initial stress): Grønnum calls stress free and lists predictably non-initial words (me'lasse, maka'roni, be'kende, pro'saisk, trompe'tist, maler'inde, bala'lajkaer, li'noleumet). It agrees with the catalog's contra note and with the existing Rischel 1970/1982 statements that placement is not fixed but predictable from phonological structure; it adds the minimal-pair count and the phrase-level stress reduction, and it does not name syllable weight explicitly.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not fixed to any one syllable ('free'): the example list has initial ('ælte, 'Panama, 'eventyr), penultimate (me'lasse, maka'roni, be'kende, maler'inde), antepenultimate (bala'lajkaer, li'noleumet) and final (pro'saisk, trompe'tist) stress. Its location is nonetheless 'to a considerable extent predictable from phonological and morphological factors', with only about 20-30 minimal stress pairs. The text does not spell out the phonological factor (vowel length / closed syllable); that mechanism comes from Rischel 1970/1982 already in the catalog, and Grønnum's examples are consistent with it, so 'weight-sensitive' is an inference, not her wording. The one thing the passage settles outright is that Danish is not fixed: initial syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress within words. p. 104 adds phrase-level stress reduction ('unit accentuation'): a verb loses stress before a bare object noun (købe 'hus vs 'købe 'huset) and in personal names only the surname is stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: About 20-30 lexical minimal pairs: billigst/bilist, August/august, tekniker/teknikker (pp. 103-104).
new_statements.identity_note: Grønnum 1998 describes the standard language as spoken in the greater Copenhagen area (p. 99: 'the variety of Danish spoken in the greater Copenhagen area serves well as the standard language'). Uneson and Schachtenhaufen 2011 work on the DanPASS corpus of spontaneous Copenhagen Danish, but say nothing about stress placement.

readall_conflicts: The only disagreement is the one the catalog already flags: Gordon 2002 codes Danish as fixed: initial syllable (initial stress), while the deciding sources describe non-fixed, largely predictable stress. Grønnum 1998 (pp. 103-104) sides against the initial coding: 'Stress is free in Danish', with predictably stressed words on the initial, penultimate, antepenultimate and final syllable. She does not name syllable weight as the phonological factor; the weight mechanism (long vowel > closed syllable > default) is Rischel's (1970, 1982), already in the catalog and the existing statements, and her example list is consistent with it. Uneson and Schachtenhaufen 2011 is silent. No source opened here supports fixed: initial syllable.

sources.citation: Rischel, Jørgen (1970). Morpheme stress in Danish. ARIPUC 4: 111-144. [Glottolog 685272; already_listed]
sources.quote: Rule 2.1.-A Syllables with shwa are never stressed. ... Rule 2.1.-B A long vowel in a stressed monomorphemic wordform carries the stress. ... Rule 2.1.-C A stressed monomorphemic wordform which contains no long vowel, takes stress on the last full vowel that is followed by a consonant. [p.122] ... Rule 2.2.-A A vowel segment containing the classificatory feature [+long] receives stress. Rule 2.2.-B If rule 2.2.-A has applied vacuously, a vowel segment followed by a consonant segment containing the classificatory feature [+long] receives stress. ... Rule 2.2.-E If rules 2.2.-A&B&C&D have applied vacuously, the last full vowel is stressed. [p.129]
sources.locator: pp. 119-123 (sec. 2.1, rules 2.1-A.D) and pp. 127-129 (sec. 2.2, rules 2.2-A.E)
sources.note: The full ordered rule set that Rischel 1982 summarises: schwa never stressed; long vowel wins; otherwise last full vowel followed by a consonant (surface rule 2.1-C) / underlying long consonant, clusters, then default 'last full vowel' (2.2-E). Lists the exception classes (French loans in a short open final, foreign names with antepenult stress, closed-final words with non-final stress such as bungalow).

sources.quote: the assumption that only sonorants project morae in coda position ... can be problematic in view of the fact that the stress system of Danish is quantity-sensitive. In Standard Danish, syllables closed by obstruents behave as if they were 'monomoraic' for the purposes of stød but nevertheless attract stress, as in, e.g., kalif [kʰaˈlif] 'caliph' (stress on rightmost closed syllable), parallel to vikar [viˈkʰɑːɐ̯] 'vicar'. ... However, whilst I cannot offer a full account of Danish stress in this paper
sources.locator: p. 261 (sec. 5.4, on submoraic structure); also p. 224 quoting Basbøll 2005:277 on stød-basis
sources.note: Paper is about dialectal short-vowel stød, not stress assignment, but states in passing that Danish stress is quantity-sensitive, that closed syllables (even obstruent-closed) attract stress, with 'stress on rightmost closed syllable' in kalif, parallel to long-vowel vikar. Consistent with the catalog's CVV/CVC weight ranking and unbounded/right-edge reading.

sources.citation: Puggaard-Rode, Rasmus, Nicolai Pharao & James Kirby. 2026. Obstruent co-intrinsic pitch and other demands on the larynx: Revisiting the mechanisms behind co-intrinsic pitch in Danish. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 56: e20, 1-32. doi:10.1017/S0025100326100930
sources.quote: In Standard Copenhagen Danish, stress in disyllabic words without stød is cued with low falling pitch on the tonic syllable and high rising pitch on the post-tonic syllable (e.g. Thorsen 1978, 1979, 1983; Dyhr 1993; Petersen 2001; Tøndering 2008). This is quite unlike in Jutland Danish, where stress is reported to be cued with high rising pitch on the tonic syllable in the absence of stød [...]. However, for reasons which are not entirely clear to us, our speaker sample from Jutland did not display the stress–pitch alignment pattern previously reported in the literature. [p. 7] Target f0 appears to be relatively low in the beginning of stressed syllables in both varieties. [p. 24]
sources.locator: pp. 7 (section 1.2.3), 17 (section 3.1, Figure 7), 24 (section 4.2); stoed as voice quality contrast p. 6 (section 1.2.2)
sources.note: marginal: Studies consonant-induced pitch effects in two Danish dialects, noting stød and regional variation in where intonational pitch peaks fall relative to stressed syllables; object is co-intrinsic pitch, not word prosody.

sources.quote: The F0 pattern associated with each prosodic stress group consists of a rise from the (low) stressed syllable to the first posttonic, followed by a fall whose extent is dependent on the number of posttonics after the first one (i.e. the fall is absent if there is only one posttonic) (Grønnum 2022, 89). [...] Copenhagen Danish lacks a default sentence accent, meaning that no one stressed syllable is more prominent than any other in utterances with neutral intonation (Grønnum 2022, 89–90).

sources.citation: Høeg, Annika. 2024. Stød and stress location in Danish: A nonce word study. Nordic Journal of Linguistics 49: 103-122. doi:10.1017/S0332586524000155
sources.quote: In Standard Danish, stød may only occur in syllables under stress (primary or secondary), with either a long vowel or a short vowel followed by a sonorant consonant. This restriction is called stød basis (Hansen 1943, Goldshtein 2023). [...] Native words in Danish are typically monosyllabic, or disyllabic with a stressed syllable followed by an unstressed syllable not containing a full vowel, mostly schwa (Basbøll 2005:400). [...] The existence of secondary stress as a phonological entity in Danish, when not being a reduced primary stress, is debated (e.g. Grønnum 2005:249, Schachtenhaufen 2022:121). [...] the fact that the speakers often pronounced these nonce words with stress on another syllable than instructed, often the penultimate syllable, implies how unintuitive it is for Danish speakers to stress the antepenultimate syllable in a simplex form.
sources.note: Production study of 336 nonce words with ultimate, penultimate or antepenultimate stress testing the stress-conditioned distribution of stød in Danish.

sources.citation: Zachariassen, Ditte. 2024. Strong Finals: A prosodic feature projecting 'more to come' in a Danish urban dialect. Nordic Journal of Linguistics 49: 68-102. doi:10.1017/S0332586524000052
sources.quote: Bi- and trisyllabic Strong Finals appear to receive stress on both the ultimate and the penultimate syllable. The stress on the ultimate syllable is realised either by means of lengthening and increased volume, as in (1) tirsdag, by means of lengthening and rising intonation, as in (4) forskellige and (5) tuneser, or by means of all three characteristics, as in (1) mandag. [...] It is possible to say that the phonological rules of stress in Standard Danish and in the regional standard are altered in the urban dialect in certain contexts. It is important to note here that by far the most common prosodic pattern in the urban dialect is Standard Danish, and that Strong Finals simply seem to be an extra prosodic resource available to the speakers to use in certain contexts.
sources.locator: pp. 78-79 (Sections 3.2 and 3.5); acoustic criteria p. 74 (Section 3.1); Standard Danish comparison pp. 74-75, 78-79
sources.note: marginal: Interactional study of a word-final lengthening/loudness/non-falling intonation feature in Aarhus urban Danish; utterance-level prosody rather than word stress.

sources.citation: Grønnum Thorsen, Nina. 1984. Variability and invariance in Danish stress group patterns. Annual Report of the Institute of Phonetics University of Copenhagen 18. doi:10.7146/aripuc.v18i.131794
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: A prosodic stress group consists of a stressed syllable and all succeeding unstressed syllables, if any. [...] Its boundaries are purely prosodically determined, lying always immediately to the left of a stressed syllable. [...] The F0 pattern associated with the prosodic stress group can be seen as an essentially invariant F0 wave, upon which the segments and syllables are superposed. In Standard Danish the stressed syllable hits the wave at the trough before the fairly steep rise to the F0 peak, which generally coincides with the first post-tonic vowel. If stressed plus first post-tonic syllable together are sufficiently short, however, the peak of the F0 wave will only be reached in the second post-tonic syllable

sources.quote: In Standard Danish the stressed vowel hits the F0 wave in the trough before the fairly steep rise to the peak, so that generally short vowels have falling movements, whereas long stressed vowels and diphthongs will be falling-rising, cf. figure 1. (p. 3) ... Take minimal stress pairs like billigst - bilist; Pallas - palads; Nanna - Nana (/'bilisd - bi'lisd -- 'palas - pa'las -- 'nana - na'na/ ... 'cheapest - motorist, the Greek goddess - palace, Danish and French girl's name). (p. 3) ... No doubt F0 rise timing is the single most effective stress location cue in this experiment, disregarding vowel duration. (p. 17) ... When everything else is equal, differences in the timing of an F0 rise between utterance initial syllables may influence the identification of the location of stress, but vowel duration - particularly the first vowel - may easily override the cue inherent in F0 rise timing. There is hardly any effect from F0 when the first vowel is sufficiently long. (p. 17) ... It seems that as far as its tonal manifestation goes, stress begins with the vowel, because - contrary to expectations, perhaps - a stressed vowel repels rather than attracts preceding homosyllabic consonants
